claims.claim: Real-world religions may not serve as analogs for evil D&D religions.
claims.source: DnD Standards (Wizards of the Coast, 2020) in the Dungeoncraft Pack 2023-12-04
claims.quote: Don’t use real-world religions as analogs for evil religions

claims.claim: Perkins and Bilsland's second principle is that an adventure needs a credible threat with logical goals the heroes can uncover and thwart.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure needs a credible threat

claims.claim: Principle four: adventures are about the here and now; the less backstory needed to set things up, the better.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure is about the here and now.

claims.claim: Principle seven: present information as concisely as possible to ease the DM's burden, reserving descriptive texture for NPCs, dungeon dressing, and treasure.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: to ease the burden on the DM

claims.claim: Principle six: information appears in the order a first-time DM needs it, with an NPC introduced before being named casually and nothing important buried.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure needs to present information in a logical

claims.claim: NPCs get character through distinctive physical features, mannerisms, and quirks the DM can roleplay.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)

claims.claim: Familiar tropes (taverns, dragons, mad wizards) are acceptable if the adventure can still surprise; writers add their own spin.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: as long as the adventure can still surprise

claims.claim: The player characters are the heroes, not spectators; fetch quests for a lazy merchant are called out as underwhelming.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: The player characters (PCs) are the heroes

claims.claim: Text must account for players' decisions and alternate outcomes, or players feel railroaded.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: players will feel “railroaded” by the plot

claims.claim: Encounters are elevated by odd monster pairings, terrain, hazards, ruses, complex motives, and plot twists.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: An adventure needs to rise above the humdrum

claims.claim: The guide's craft advice is to read many good adventures, as novelists read novels.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)
claims.quote: The more good D&D adventures you read, the

claims.claim: AL writers must not decide in advance how the adventure ends, even in a 2- or 4-hour slot.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)

claims.feature: Chicago edition cited by the design guide
claims.claim: The design guide still cites Chicago 16th edition, one edition behind the style guide's 17th, showing the bundle's documents were not synchronized.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)

claims.claim: The design guide points writers to the House Style Guide for grammar and to the Adventure Format Template for layout, which is where boxed-text rules live.
claims.source: Adventure Design Guide ('Writing Adventures', Chris Perkins & Greg Bilsland)

claims.claim: The Forgotten Realms guide sets a hopeful tone in which the good guys eventually win, contrasted with cynical Greyhawk and tragic Dragonlance.
claims.source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
claims.quote: The Forgotten Realms is a hopeful setting.
